RBI Monetary Policy: Repo Rate, CRR, SLR and Inflation Targeting

Monetary policy is how the RBI manages interest rates and the money supply to control inflation and support growth. This guide explains each tool and how a rate change reaches you. The rates themselves change, so check the RBI for current values.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Goals and who decides

India has a flexible inflation targeting framework: the target for CPI inflation is 4%, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%. A six-member Monetary Policy Committee, three from the RBI and three appointed by the government, sets the repo rate. It normally meets at least four times a year, in practice about every two months.

The tools of monetary policy

ToolWhat it isIf raised
Repo rateRate at which RBI lends to banksLoans get costlier, and demand slows
Reverse repo rateRate at which RBI borrows from banksBanks park more with RBI
Standing deposit facility (SDF)Collateral-free RBI borrowing from banks, the floor of the rate corridorAbsorbs surplus money
Marginal standing facility (MSF)Emergency overnight borrowing for banks, the ceiling of the corridorEmergency money costs more
CRRShare of deposits kept with RBI as cashLess money for banks to lend
SLRShare of deposits kept in liquid assetsLess money for banks to lend
Open market operationsRBI buying or selling government securitiesSelling takes money out of the system

Quantitative and qualitative tools

Quantitative tools such as the repo rate, CRR, SLR and open market operations affect the total amount of money. Qualitative tools, such as margin requirements on loans, moral suasion and credit rationing, steer where the credit goes.

Expansionary and contractionary policy

BasisExpansionary (dovish)Contractionary (hawkish)
WhenGrowth is weakInflation is high
ActionCut rates, add liquidityRaise rates, absorb liquidity
LoansCheaperCostlier
RiskInflationSlower growth

How a rate change reaches you

  • The RBI changes the repo rate.
  • Banks' cost of money changes.
  • Loan rates change: floating-rate retail loans linked to an external benchmark such as the repo rate adjust at their reset date, and FD rates follow in time.
  • People and businesses borrow and spend more or less.
  • Demand, and therefore inflation and growth, respond over several months.

Effects on markets

  • Bonds: yields usually fall when rates are cut, so bond prices rise.
  • Shares: lower rates tend to help, especially for banks, autos and real estate.
  • Currency: higher rates can attract foreign money and support the rupee.
  • Fixed deposits: rates tend to fall after cuts, so savers look for longer lock-ins beforehand.

Monetary and fiscal policy

Monetary policy is run by the RBI, using interest rates and liquidity. Fiscal policy is run by the government, using taxes and spending, and is covered in our GDP and fiscal policy guide. They work best when they pull in the same direction.

Exam and interview questions

What is the difference between repo rate and reverse repo rate?

The repo rate is what banks pay when they borrow from the RBI. The reverse repo rate is what the RBI pays when it borrows from banks.

What is the difference between CRR and SLR?

CRR is kept with the RBI as cash and earns no interest. SLR is kept by the banks themselves in liquid assets such as government securities, which do earn interest.

What is India's inflation target?

4% CPI inflation, with a tolerance band of 2% to 6%, under the flexible inflation targeting framework.

Why does the RBI raise rates when inflation is high?

Higher rates make borrowing costlier and saving more attractive, which cools demand and eases pressure on prices.
